awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Exact Optimal and Data-Adaptive Algorithms and Tools for Differential Privacy
awd_abstract_narration:
This project is motivated by the increasing public concerns on privacy issues, new legislations and the high demand for privacy enhancing technologies such as differential privacy (DP) in applications from both private and public sectors. The overarching theme of the project is to address the pressing new challenges that arise as differential privacy transforms from a theoretical construct into a practical technology. The project advances the state-of-the-art of research in the area of DP, and contributes to privacy education. On the research front, the project develops new algorithms and analytical tools that enable more precise privacy accounting and higher utility in DP. On the education front, the project involves training future leaders in DP areas, creating educational materials and expanding an open-source software library called autodp that makes state-of-the-art differentially private computation more accessible. Collectively, the integrated research and educational activities contribute to ongoing collaborative efforts in building innovative applications of differential privacy.
 
The project has three main components in use-inspired fundamental research. The first component unifies the recent breakthroughs in DP, such as, Renyi DP, moments accountant, f-DP and produce an intermediate functional representation that allows lossless conversions among these representations. The second component focuses on investigating the stronger privacy properties permitted by the structures of the actual data, and addressing the dilemma of interpreting  worst-case privacy on average-case data. The third component focuses on using a public dataset to ``denoise'' the private data releases or to facilitate private machine learning. The outputs of the research will be broadly shared through integration in autodp library, and will be integrated in courses.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Differential privacy is a rigorous way to learn from sensitive data while limiting what can be inferred about any one person. It can help organizations draw useful conclusions from information such as medical records, education data, or online activity without exposing individual records. The central goal of this CAREER project was to make differential privacy more accurate, adaptable, and practical: to waste less of the limited “privacy budget,” to adjust protection to the data and the task, and to give practitioners trustworthy tools for building private systems.

The project advanced the mathematical foundations of privacy accounting—the process used to determine the total privacy risk when a system performs many data analyses. The research developed an exact, lossless way to translate among several widely used descriptions of differential privacy. This unified view led to more accurate accounting and reduced unnecessary noise. The ideas were implemented in AutoDP, an open-source software library that lets researchers and developers describe, combine, and analyze private algorithms. AutoDP, together with public tutorials, examples, and course materials, lowered the barrier to using modern privacy analysis correctly.

A second group of results made privacy protection more responsive to real data. Standard guarantees are designed for the worst possible data set and can therefore be overly conservative. The project developed methods for privately checking whether a proposed analysis is safe on the data at hand, measuring privacy protection for individual records, selecting useful models or statistics, and reusing predictions while controlling cumulative privacy risk. These results improve the balance between privacy and usefulness while retaining formal guarantees.

The project also broadened the range of learning tasks that can be performed privately. It produced new methods and analyses for classification, regression, data valuation, reinforcement learning, online decision-making, and the private fine-tuning and use of large models. Later work showed how public, already-trained representations can make private learning more effective; how an approximate privacy guarantee can be converted to a stronger, failure-free form through randomized post-processing; and how a retrieval-augmented language model can answer many questions about a private document collection while controlling the total privacy loss. Together, these contributions show that rigorous privacy can be built into increasingly capable artificial-intelligence systems rather than treated as an afterthought.

As privacy tools enter unfamiliar settings, correct implementation and verification become critical. The project helped create DPCheatSheet, which uses worked solutions and carefully designed erroneous examples to teach people how to implement differential privacy with assistance from language models. It also contributed DPrivBench, a benchmark that tests whether language models can reason correctly about privacy guarantees. These projects identify where current systems succeed, where they make subtle mistakes, and how people and automated tools can work together more safely.

The award’s broader impacts include open-source software, freely available papers and teaching materials, and extensive dissemination through conference presentations, workshops, invited talks, and the NSF Secure and Trustworthy Cyberspace principal-investigator meeting. The project supported and mentored doctoral students, a postdoctoral researcher, and undergraduate researchers, including students from groups underrepresented in computing. Project results were incorporated into a graduate course on differential privacy and into student projects that connected formal privacy ideas with practical telemetry and machine-learning applications. Trainees presented their work at leading research conferences and specialized privacy workshops, helping them develop as independent researchers.

Overall, the project produced a collection of mathematical methods, algorithms, software, benchmarks, and educational resources that make strong privacy guarantees more accurate, understandable, and usable. These outcomes support the responsible use of sensitive data and help prepare researchers and practitioners to build data-driven and AI systems that protect the people represented in their data.
